# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden and a Halden Subset

This is the most informative document in the set. It directly tests the three questions left open: whether the gain persists, whether the meetings explanation holds up, and whether timesheets understate work. It also corrects both of the previous overclaims.

- **Novelty.** Against Varga & Holm, a gain remains at 24 months under the strictest design in the literature.
- **Decay.** Against the meta-analysis, the gain did decline, and the review's "no decay" evidence came entirely from weak designs. That confirms the concern I raised about those four long-follow-up studies.

The main weaknesses are a summary that compares two different measures, a mediation analysis that claims more precision and independence than it has, an unclear definition of the new log-based hours measure, and a cost figure that doesn't match its own inputs.

## Arithmetic check

These are correct:

- **Output per hour, timesheets.** 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8%.
- **Output per hour, system logs.** 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers.** 34.9 / 40.3 is −13.4%, and 0.968 / 0.866 = 1.118, so +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares.** 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%.
- **Meeting cut.** The difference-in-differences is 3.5 − 0.2 = 3.3 hours, matching the month-six figure.

Two figures don't follow:

- **The cost of the counter arm.** Restoring output after an 11.4% fall per FTE needs about 1/0.886, or 12–13% more staff, as the report says. At unchanged pay, cost per contact then rises by about 12%, not 9%. The 9% needs an explanation, such as cheaper new hires or spreading of fixed costs, or it is an error.
- **"About a quarter".** On the like-for-like timesheet measure, the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%, roughly a fifth. If you compare 12.5% with the logs figure of 8.5%, it is about a third. "About a quarter" matches neither comparison.

## 1. The headline compares two different measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". But 12.5% was measured with timesheets and 8.5% with system logs. The body handles this correctly: 12.5% → 9.8% on timesheets, plus 8.5% on the stricter logs measure at 24 months only. The summary should say the same. As written, it overstates the decline over time by mixing it with the change of measure.

Two further points about the decline:

- **It isn't formally tested.** The intervals (6.9–18.4% and 4.6–15.2%) overlap heavily. The decline is plausible but not demonstrated, and a test of the change within the same offices should be reported.
- **It could partly come from the control group.** Two control offices cut their meetings from month 15 and improved their output per hour by 4.1%. That narrows the gap between arms without the treated offices getting any worse. Part of the apparent decay may be control offices catching up. Reporting the levels for each arm over time, and the estimate with those two offices excluded, would separate the two explanations.

## 2. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms" suggests

- **It isn't independent replication.** The meetings hypothesis came from these same offices. Registering the test at month 11 means it can't have been shaped by the 24-month outcome data. But the same seven treated offices produced the original observation, and months 1–11 overlap with the data that generated it.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices.** The report claims a "larger sample of office-months", but office-months within an office are correlated. A mediation interval as narrow as 28–66% from 14 clusters looks too precise unless it was computed with small-cluster methods. The method should be stated.
- **Meeting cuts weren't randomised.** The authors acknowledge that mediation needs no unmeasured confounding. The obvious confounder is manager quality: managers who cut meetings may also improve output in other ways.
- **The baseline meeting data need a source.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six, as an unregistered extra. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). If these were reconstructed from historical calendars, the report should say so and say how complete they are.

So the fair summary is that the meetings explanation survived a pre-registered test it could have failed. That is real progress over a seven-office correlation, but it is not confirmation.

## 3. What do the system logs actually measure?

The logs are described as "active log-in time on the case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases". If that means time spent on cases only, the numbers don't fit together:

- At baseline, treated staff worked 37.9 timesheet hours, with 7.4 in meetings, leaving about 30.5 hours of non-meeting time.
- At 24 months, timesheet hours were about 33.4, with 3.9 in meetings, leaving about 29.5 hours of non-meeting time.

That is a fall of only about 3% in non-meeting time. Case-only logs should then fall by about 3%, not 11%.

If the logs instead include meeting time, the description is wrong. In either case the definition matters for the mechanism.

- **If meetings are outside the denominator**, cutting them can't raise output per logged hour simply by removing low-value time. It would have to work through fewer interruptions while doing case work.
- **If logs miss offline work**, such as phone calls or paper files, they aren't strictly the "stricter" measure the report treats them as.

## 4. The Halden follow-up

- **Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations contacted responded. The nine that didn't are plausibly more likely to have reverted or struggled. The authors' "survivors twice over" caveat is right, and arguably understated.
- **Which baseline was used.** The baseline of 40.3 hours is exactly the average for Halden's 27 time-tracked organisations. The report should confirm that all 11 continuers have time tracking and that 40.3 is their own baseline, not the figure for the larger group.
- **A discretionary organisation reverted.** A marketing agency left because of client deadlines. That is a useful counterexample to treating discretionary and coverage-bound as a clean split, which the meta-analysis noted is often a mix within one organisation.
- **The attrition correction is still missing.** R. Okafor is a Halden author. Varga & Holm showed that the Halden working paper misdescribed its withdrawals, and this report would have been a natural place to acknowledge or correct that.

## 5. Handled well

- **Stopping the counter arm.** The county ended it at month 12, and the report records that rather than leaving it out. The waiting times (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes) settle the coverage-bound question about as clearly as one county can.
- **The unplanned meeting audit.** It is honestly framed: two offices, uncontrolled, suggestive. The authors also state the open design question correctly: no arm reorganised work without cutting hours, so the trial can't tell whether the hours cut is necessary or only a catalyst.
- **The response to the earlier papers.** Section 5 gives Varga & Holm credit for the measurement problems they identified before rejecting their conclusion. It also checks the meta-analysis's supplementary table rather than merely asserting a problem.

## What the four documents now support together

1. **In discretionary work**, a 20% cut in scheduled hours becomes a cut of about 11–13% in actual hours. Output per worker ends up about 2–4% below control. Output per actual hour is about 8–10% higher at two years, somewhat less than at nine months. The evidence comes mostly from one randomised public-sector trial, so generalising remains a limitation.
2. **In coverage-bound work**, the scheme fails on service unless staff are added. Adding them raises cost per unit by roughly 10–12%.
3. **Mechanism.** A substantial share of the gain appears to come from cutting meetings, with fatigue a smaller contributor and about a third unexplained. Whether reorganising without cutting hours could achieve most of the gain is the key open question. It needs a three-arm trial: reduced hours, reorganisation only, and control.
4. **Still missing is a full cost–benefit calculation.** Output per FTE about 3% lower at the same pay raises cost per case by about 3.5%. Against that are sick days down 27% and resignations nearly halved. None of the papers puts a value on those savings, and that calculation would decide the practical question for most employers.
